titre: Much, many, a lot of, a few, a little
intro: These words talk about quantity: a large or a small amount. The right choice depends on two questions: is the noun countable or uncountable, and is the sentence positive, negative or a question?
objectifs: Choose between much (uncountable) and many (plural countable).
Use a lot of / lots of in positive sentences, and much / many mostly in negatives and questions.
Understand the difference between a few / a little (some: positive) and few / little (not enough: negative).
Ask How much…? / How many…? and use too much, too many, so many, plenty of.

sections.titre: Countable or uncountable: the starting point
texte: A countable noun can be counted: one apple, two apples; it has a plural. An uncountable noun can't be counted directly: water, money, time, bread, information; it has no plural and takes a singular verb (lesson 59 looks at these nouns and their traps).
“Many” and “a few” go with plural countable nouns. “Much” and “a little” go with uncountable nouns. “A lot of” and “lots of” go with both.

lignes: many books / a lot of books
much money / a lot of money

sections.titre: Much / many or a lot of?
texte: In positive sentences, everyday English uses “a lot of” or “lots of” (more informal): I've got a lot of friends. She drinks lots of coffee. “Much” in a positive sentence sounds very formal or strange: don't say “I have much money”.
In negatives and questions, “much” and “many” are natural: I haven't got much time. Are there many people? “A lot of” is also possible: Have you got a lot of work?

“Many” is a little easier than “much” in positive sentences, especially in writing: Many people think that… And after “too, so, as, very”, much and many are normal in positive sentences: There are too many cars. I've got so much work!
exemples: There are a lot of tourists in Bruges in August.
We don't have much money this month.
I've got so much homework tonight!
so much in a positive sentence.
sections.note: With no noun after it, say “a lot” (not “a lot of”): I like it a lot. Thanks a lot. “Much” alone is very common in negatives: I don't eat much.

sections.titre: A few / a little: some, a small amount
texte: “A few” + plural countable noun means a small number, but enough: I've got a few friends in Lyon. “A little” + uncountable noun means a small amount: Can I have a little milk?
“A little” can also go before an adjective, or alone: I'm a little tired. In speaking, “a bit” is more common: I'm a bit tired, a bit of sugar.

sections.titre: Few / little without “a”: a negative meaning
texte: Without “a”, the meaning changes: “few” and “little” mean “not many, not much, not enough”, with a negative idea. Compare: I've got a few friends (some friends, that's OK) / I've got few friends (not many friends, that's sad).
These forms are a little formal. In speaking, people often say “not many / not much”: I haven't got many friends. There isn't much hope.
“Plenty of” (more than enough) goes with both kinds of nouns: We've got plenty of time. There are plenty of chairs.
“Too much / too many” = more than is good or necessary: too much sugar, too many people. Don't confuse it with “very much”: I like it very much, where “much” is an adverb.
“How much” is also used to ask a price: How much is this jacket? How much does it cost?
exemples: Don't hurry. We've got plenty of time.
There's too much noise in this café.
How much are the tickets? — Twelve euros each.

formule: many / a few + plural · much / a little + uncountable · a lot of + both · much / many mostly in negatives and questions
prononciation: “a lot of” joins: /ə ˈlɒt əv/, often /əˈlɒdə/ in fast American English (“a lotta”).
“much” /mʌtʃ/ and “many” /ˈmeni/: the a in many sounds like the e in “bed”.
“a few” /ə ˈfjuː/: the “a” is weak but you must say it, or the meaning becomes negative (few).
“a little” /ə ˈlɪtl/: in American English, the t sounds like a quick d (/ˈlɪdl/).
In “How much is it?”, stress MUCH; the voice goes down at the end.
erreurs: I have a lot of friends.
Many for countable nouns; in positive sentences a lot of is more natural.
How many money have you got?
How much money have you got?
I've got a lot of homeworks.
I've got a lot of homework.
I like it a lot of.
With no noun after it: a lot.
Can I have a few water?
Can I have a little water?
I speak little English, it's fine.

dialogue.contexte: Two friends prepare dinner for eight people in their shared flat in Montréal.
lignes: How many people are coming tonight?
Eight. So we need a lot of rice. How much rice have we got?
Not much. Only a little. And there are only a few tomatoes.
a little rice, a few tomatoes.
OK, I'll go to the shop. Do we need many drinks?
No, we've got plenty of juice. But buy a few bottles of water.
And bread? We haven't got much.
Buy two baguettes. Don't buy too many sweets this time!
Ha ha, OK. I've got very little money anyway.

mots: We need a small quantity of sugar.

how much there is (with uncountable nouns)
how many there are (with countable nouns)
as much or as many as you need

more than two, but not many

items: I need ___ help with this exercise.

exercices.consigne: Choose the most natural form in speaking.
items: I've got (much / a lot of) work this week.
There are (too much / too many) people here.
Thank you (a lot / a lot of)!

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: How many money do you need?
How much money do you need?
I have much friends in Ghent.
I have a lot of friends in Ghent.
There's too many sugar in this tea.
There's too much sugar in this tea.
Can you give me a few information?
Can you give me a little information? / Can you give me some information?
We've got a lot of homeworks.
We've got a lot of homework.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the word in brackets, keeping the same meaning.
items: The roads are quite empty today. (not much traffic)
I know three or four people in Toronto. (a few)
I've got a few friends in Toronto. / I know a few people in Toronto.
What is the number of people who work here? (How many)
We have more than enough time. (plenty of)
We've got plenty of time. / We have plenty of time.

exercices.consigne: Describe your town or your kitchen in five sentences with much, many, a lot of, a few and a little.
items: There are a lot of restaurants in my town, but there aren't many parks. There isn't much traffic at night. In my kitchen there are a few apples and a little cheese. I haven't got much time to cook during the week.

a_retenir: many / a few / few + plural; much / a little / little + uncountable; a lot of + both.
Positive: a lot of; negatives and questions: much / many.
a few / a little = some (positive); few / little = not enough (negative).
How many + plural? How much + uncountable? How much is it? = price.
too much / too many = more than is good; plenty of = more than enough; with no noun: a lot.
